title: The greater Saccaka
hookLine: pleasant feeling does not invade his mind; the story of the austerities retold

lines: HAS PLEASURE EVER CARRIED YOU AWAY?
THE BUDDHA TELLS HIS OWN STORY.
cards: It's morning in Vesali. The Buddha has dressed and taken his bowl to go for alms, and here comes Saccaka, walking up for another round. This time he's not boasting.
He has a sharper question, almost a personal one. Some teachers train the body, he says, and some train the mind. Have you ever felt a pleasant feeling so strong it carried your mind away?
Or a pain so strong it did? The Buddha answers with his own story.

teach.b: In the thirty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the Buddha tells Saccaka his own story of the austerities.

He pressed his tongue to his palate and crushed his mind with his mind, until sweat ran from his armpits. He held his breath until his head felt split by a sharp sword, and his belly felt carved by a butcher's knife.

teach.h: THE AUSTERITIES, TOLD IN HIS OWN WORDS
teach.b: He ate less and less, until his limbs looked like knotted vine stems, his spine stood out like a string of beads, his ribs like the rafters of a ruined shed, and his eyes sank like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well.
After each of these, he says the same strange line: the painful feeling that arose in me did not invade my mind and remain. He could bear it. But bearing it didn't free him.
Then he remembered a day in childhood.
His father was busy at work, and he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind settled into a quiet, wholesome joy.
He asked himself: why am I afraid of that kind of happiness, which has nothing to do with sense pleasures? I'm not afraid of it. So he ate some rice.

The five companions left in disgust. Then came the deep absorptions, and through the watches of a night, awakening. And through all of it, he tells Saccaka, the pleasant feeling, too, did not invade his mind and remain.

teach.h: PAIN CAME, JOY CAME, NEITHER STAYED

how: Buddhist teachers retell the austerities, the memory under the rose-apple tree and the bowl of rice as the turn toward the middle way, and meditators practice letting pleasant and painful feelings arise without being carried away by them.

o: a king who gave the monks a great meal
the debater who heard the Buddha's own story
a teacher of breath control in Vesali

games.q: the austerities, in his words — tap the pairs.
p: like the rafters of a ruined shed
like water in a deep well
a childhood memory of quiet joy

s: the austerities freed him because he could bear the pain
he could bear it: the pain didn't invade his mind. but bearing it didn't free him.
a childhood memory helped turn him toward the middle way
he remembered sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree while his father worked, his mind quiet and glad.
his five companions approved when he ate rice
they left him in disgust, thinking he had given up.

games.q: you've fasted until your ribs show like rafters. you remember a day of quiet, wholesome joy under a tree as a child. you're afraid of that happiness. what do you decide?
o: fear it: any pleasure is a trap.
there's no need to fear a happiness that has nothing to do with sense pleasures.
games.why: he asks why he's afraid of that happiness, and decides he isn't. he eats some rice, his companions walk out, and the path to awakening opens.

practice: Find one pleasant thing in this moment, warmth in your hands, the chair holding you, the quiet, and let yourself enjoy it fully.
Then notice the little lean in the mind that says more, keep this, and watch the pleasant feeling stay or fade on its own while you enjoy it without holding it.

wordCard.voice: Saccaka. The long discourse where the Buddha tells of his austerities, the rose-apple tree, and a mind that pain and pleasure could visit but not take over.

carryVoice: Your line: it didn't invade. Pain and pleasure can visit without moving in. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the greater discourse to Saccaka)
